Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 100, verse 1–11:

Meccan, though it is said to be Medinan, and its verses are 11 [revealed after the afternoon prayer]. In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful.

He swears by the warhorses that run and snort. Ḍabḥ (snorting) is the sound of their breathing when they run. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he imitated it and said: "ḥ ḥ." ʿAntara said:

"The horses strive (yakdaḥ) when they snort into the basins of death, snorting."

[[Al-kadḥ: exertion in running; al-ḍabḥ: expelling breath with a sound other than neighing or whinnying. Ibn ʿAbbas related it in his tafsir and said: "ḥ ḥ." He likened death to a torrent by way of metaphor (al-makniyya), and "the basins" is an imaginative representation (takhyīl) of that.]] The accusative of ḍabḥan is either "they snort a snorting" (yaḍbaḥna ḍabḥan), or it depends on al-ʿādiyāt, as if it were said: "wal-ḍābiḥāt," because snorting occurs together with running. [[Maḥmūd said: "He swears by the warhorses that run and snort, and ḍabḥ is the sound of their breathing..." Aḥmad said: He did not mention the wisdom of using a verb coordinated with a noun. We say: He coordinated fa-atharna with the noun al-ʿādiyāt and what follows it because they are active participles, which give the meaning of the verb. The wisdom of this coordinated verb following an active participle is to depict these actions in the soul, for depiction is achieved by placing a verb after a noun, because of the contrast between them. This is more eloquent than depiction by consistent nouns. Likewise is depiction by the present tense after the past, and its best examples have already passed, the nearest of which is the words of Ibn Maʿdikarib:

"For I met the ghoul rushing in a desert like a page, a smooth plain,
So I struck it without dismay, and it fell prostrate, both hands and neck."]] Or it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), meaning: snorting. Then fal-mūriyāt tūrī nār al-ḥabāḥib [[His saying "tūrī nār al-ḥabāḥib": al-Ḥabāḥib is the name of a stingy man who would kindle only a weak fire for fear of guests, so they made him a proverb until they said: "the fire of al-Ḥabāḥib" for what the horses strike with their hooves. From al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] which is what flies off from their hooves, qadḥan. Qādiḥāt (striking), ṣākkāt (hitting) with their hooves the stones. Al-qadḥ is the striking.

Al-Īrāʾ is the bringing out of fire. One says: "qadaḥa fa-awrā" (he struck and kindled), and "qadaḥa fa-aṣlada" [[His saying "fa-aṣlada": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ṣalada al-zand means when the firestick makes a sound but does not bring out sparks; and aṣlada al-rajul means his firestick was barren. (ʿ)]]. Qadḥan is in the accusative by the same that governs ḍabḥan. Fal-mughīrāt tughīr ʿalā al-ʿadū ṣubḥan: they raid the enemy at the time of dawn (ṣubḥ). Fa-atharna bihi naqʿan: they raised thereby dust, thus they stirred at that time dust. Fa-wasaṭna bihi: they penetrated thereby, at that time, or by the dust, meaning they pierced the dust into the gathering. Fa-wasaṭna jamʿan: a gathering of the enemy's hosts.

Or: fa-wasaṭna, being entangled with it, a gathering of the enemy's hosts; its "wasaṭ" is the same as its "tawassuṭ" (penetration). It is said: the pronoun refers to the place of the raid. It is also said: it refers to the enemy indicated by al-ʿādiyāt. It is permissible to take al-naqʿ to mean the outcry, from his (peace be upon him) saying: "As long as there is no naqʿ or laqlaqa" [[I have not found it as a marfūʿ (raised) report. Al-Bukhari mentioned it in al-Janāʾiz as a suspended report from ʿUmar. He said: "Let them weep for Abū Sulaymān as long as there is no naqʿ or laqlaqa." He said: al-naqʿ is dust on the head, and al-laqlaqa is the voice. ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Ḥākim, Ibn Saʿd, Abū ʿUbayd and al-Ḥarbī in al-Gharīb all connected it through the chain of al-Aʿmash from Abū Wāʾil who said: "It was said to ʿUmar: Women of the Banū al-Mughīra have gathered in the house of Khālid ibn al-Walīd weeping over him, and we dislike that they should harm you. So if you forbade them..." He said: "There is no harm for them to shed some of their tears for Abū Sulaymān, a bucket or two, as long as there is no naqʿ or laqlaqa." In the report of Ibn Saʿd: Wakīʿ said: al-naqʿ is tearing, and al-laqlaqa is the voice. Some said: raising dust on the head and tearing the collars. As for laqlaqa, it is intense shouting. I have not heard any disagreement about it. Al-Ḥarbī related from al-Aṣmaʿī: al-naqʿ is shouting. And from Abū Salama: it is placing dust on the head.]] And the words of Labīd:

"So when a true cry rises (yanqaʿ)... Their calling (jalabūhu) with a sound of jingling and a buzz."

[[Labīd ibn Rabīʿa. Jalaba ʿalā faraspihi and ajlaba: when he shouted to it and urged it to race ahead. Jalaba (with doubled lām): a sound. Al-jaras: a faint sound. Al-zajal: a sound like the humming of bees. He says: "So when a true cry for war rises, the shouters of it are a company with jingling," and it is a substitute for the subject of jalabūhu, or it follows the dialect of "akalūnī al-barāghīth" (the fleas ate me). The meaning: the low sound is constant with them, unlike the raised sound. It is permissible that "jalabūhu" is the answer of the condition; and it is permissible that it is an attribute of ṣurāKH, and the answer of the condition is what follows it, and this is closer than the first.]]

That is: they stirred up against them in the raid a shouting and clamour. [[His saying "ṣibāḥan wa jalaba": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-jalb and al-jalaba: sounds. (ʿ)]] Abū Ḥaywa read: fa-atharna with doubled (tashdīd), meaning: they displayed dust by it, because al-taʾthīr has the meaning of displaying. Or ṯawarna was changed to waṯarna, and the waw changed to a hamza. It was also read: fa-wasaṭna with doubled, for transitivity; the bāʾ is added for emphasis, like His saying: "and bring it to them" (wa-utū bihi), and it is an intensification in wasaṭna.

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: I was sitting in al-Ḥijr when a man came and asked me about al-ʿādiyāt ḍabḥan, and I explained them as horses. He went to ʿAlī, who was beneath the water-spout of Zamzam, and asked him and mentioned to him what I had said. He said: "Bring him to me." When I stood before him, he said: "You give fatwās to people about what you have no knowledge of. By God, the first raid in Islam was Badr, and with us there were only two horses: a horse for al-Zubayr and a horse for al-Miqdād." Al-ʿādiyāt ḍabḥan are the camels from ʿArafa to Muzdalifa, and from Muzdalifa to Minā. [[Related by al-Ṭabarī and al-Ḥākim from the narration of Abū Ṣakhr from Abū Muʿāwiya al-Bajalī from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas; and al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn Mardawayh related it from this route.]] If the report is sound, then ḍabḥ is used metaphorically for camels, as al-mashāfir and al-ḥāfir are used for humans, the two lips for the young camel, the thafr for the bull-cow [[His saying "li-l-mahr wa al-thafr al-thawra": al-thafr is the pudendum of beasts like the vulva of a she-camel, and it is sometimes used metaphorically for other things. Al-thawra is the feminine of thawr. Al-Akhṭal said: "May God repay on our behalf the two one-eyed men with courtesy, and Farwa, the thafr of the crooked-mouthed bull-cow." Farwa is a man's name, and al-mutaḍājim is one whose mouth is crooked. From a margin note. (ʿ)]] and the like. It was said: ḍabḥ is only for the horse, the dog, and the fox. It was said: ḍabḥ means ḍabʿ (hyena-like panting); one says: "ḍabaḥat al-ibil wa ḍabaʿat" when they stretch their flanks in the journey; but this is not established. And jamʿ is Muzdalifa.

If you ask: upon what is fa-atharna coordinated? I say: upon the verb whose place the active participle has taken, for the meaning is: "those who ran and so struck fire, and so raided, and so stirred dust."

Al-kanūd: the ungrateful. One says: "kanada al-niʿma kanūdan" (he was ungrateful for the blessing). From it the tribe Kinda is named, because he (their ancestor) was ungrateful to his father and separated from him. It is related from al-Kalbī: al-kanūd in the language of Kinda: the disobedient; in the language of Banū Mālik: the stingy; in the language of Muḍar and Rabīʿa: the ungrateful. He means: he is, toward the blessing of his Lord, exceedingly ungrateful, for his neglect in giving thanks for the blessings of other than God is a neglect close to the blessing itself, because the greatest blessing bestowed on man is that of his parents; then their greatness, beside the least of God's blessings, is small and slight. And innahu ʿalā dhālika (and he, upon that, in his ungratefulness) la-shahīd: he bears witness against himself and cannot deny it, because his condition is manifest. It was also said: wa-innahu... wa-inna Allāh ʿalā kanūdih la-shāhid, by way of threat.

Al-khayr: wealth, from His saying: "if he leaves wealth (khayran)." Al-shadīd: the stingy, the one who withholds. One says: "fulān shadīd wa mutashaddid." Ṭarafa said:

"I see death selecting the noble, and choosing
The precious wealth of the sinful, the stingy one."

[[By Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd in his Muʿallaqa. Iʿtāma: to choose by choice. Al-ʿaqīla of everything is its noblest. He says: "I see death choosing the noble and taking them, and choosing the most precious wealth of the stingy, tight-fisted one, leaving it behind." It was also said: it takes that too.]]

He means: and it is, because of love of wealth and because spending it is burdensome to him, a stingy withholder. One says: "he is shadīd for this matter, and qawī for it," when he is able for it and controls it. Or he meant: because of love of good things, he is not cheerful and open, but tight and contracted.

buʿthira (is scattered) — ba'atha. It is read: buḥthira, and buḥthira and ḥuṣṣila, on the forms of their verbs in the active. Ḥuṣṣila with lightening. The meaning of ḥuṣṣila: it was gathered in the scrolls, that is, it was made manifest, collected. It was also said: it distinguished its good from its evil. From it the sieve is called al-muḥaṣṣil.

The meaning of His knowing them on the Day of Resurrection is that He recompenses them according to the measures of their deeds, because that is the effect of His knowledge of them. Abū al-Sammāl read: inna Rabbahum bihim yawmaʾidhin la-khabīr.

From the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him): "Whoever recites the sūrah al-ʿĀdiyāt, he is given the reward of ten good deeds, according to the number of those who spent the night at Muzdalifa and witnessed the gathering." [[Related by al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.]]

And innahu ʿalā dhālika (and he, upon that, in his ungratefulness) la-shahīd: he bears witness against himself and cannot deny it, because his condition is manifest. It was also said: wa-innahu... wa-inna Allāh ʿalā kanūdih la-shāhid, by way of threat.

Al-khayr: wealth, from His saying: "if he leaves wealth (khayran)." Al-shadīd: the stingy, the one who withholds. One says: "fulān shadīd wa mutashaddid." Ṭarafa said:

"I see death selecting the noble, and choosing
The precious wealth of the sinful, the stingy one."

[[By Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd in his Muʿallaqa. Iʿtāma: to choose by choice. Al-ʿaqīla of everything is its noblest. He says: "I see death choosing the noble and taking them, and choosing the most precious wealth of the stingy, tight-fisted one, leaving it behind." It was also said: it takes that too.]]

He means: and it is, because of love of wealth and because spending it is burdensome to him, a stingy withholder. Or he meant by al-shadīd: the strong, and that because of love of wealth and preference for this world and its pursuit, he is strong and capable, while for love of the worship of God and thanks for His blessing he is weak and lax. One says: "he is shadīd for this matter, and qawī for it," when he is able for it and controls it. Or he meant: because of love of good things, he is not cheerful and open, but tight and contracted.

buʿthira (is scattered) — ba'atha. It is read: buḥthira, and buḥthira and ḥuṣṣila, on the forms of their verbs in the active. Ḥuṣṣila with lightening. The meaning of ḥuṣṣila: it was gathered in the scrolls, that is, it was made manifest, collected. It was also said: it distinguished its good from its evil. From it the sieve is called al-muḥaṣṣil.

The meaning of His knowing them on the Day of Resurrection is that He recompenses them according to the measures of their deeds, because that is the effect of His knowledge of them. Abū al-Sammāl read: inna Rabbahum bihim yawmaʾidhin la-khabīr.

From the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him): "Whoever recites the sūrah al-ʿĀdiyāt, he is given the reward of ten good deeds, according to the number of those who spent the night at Muzdalifa and witnessed the gathering."
